To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) financial inclusion is the dominant policy paradigm in development finance, replacing microfinance; (b) financial inclusion is a policy that is being pushed by a coalition of card companies (card crusaders), and (c) this coalition is pushing for an end of physical cash and a full digitalisation of the poor's money; and (d) this is being done in order to capitalise on poor people's daily transaction costs, to monetize the big data generated by poor people's money

the digitalization of money is being pushed by a coalition of actors that includes card crusaders, and that these actors are pursuing three holy grails of digital financial inclusion: to capitalize on everyday transaction costs; to use big data to sell and analyse the poor; and to exert greater control over poor people's finances.
the financial inclusion agenda, which is currently being pursued in many developing countries, is a moral crusade to promote the use of digital money and the elimination of cash among the poor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the moral economy of the digitalisation of poor peoples money.
the moral crusade over digitalising poor money.
the moral and political economy of financial inclusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
financial inclusion is a new and important development policy, but it is also a new and important form of financialisation, with all the risks that entails.
the digital turn in financial inclusion is a major step in the wrong direction, and that it is time to stop the crusade.
the turn to digital finance and the end of physical cash is not about the poor, but about the rich.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the financial inclusion agenda is not a new one, but that the digital turn has brought new actors to the space and has given them a new set of tools.
financial inclusion is a moral crusade, and that this crusade is not in the interest of the poor.
the financial inclusion movement is an important step forward for the poor in many ways, but it is also a step back in other ways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
financial inclusion is being driven by a profit oriented agenda, with the poor being positioned as the new market to be captured.
digital money is not neutral and should not be seen as a panacea for the financial needs of the poor.
financial inclusion is not about inclusion, but about the exclusion of cash.
